What the relay does there, read from its code:

- a face login is kept on your member row and survives a restart, but it expires after a stretch of no use; then it asks again
- the login mail goes out at most once a minute and five times an hour; past that it sends nothing and says nothing
- a mail that fails to send is dropped without a word in the log, so a broken mail driver looks exactly like this

- each use moves the relay's own deadline 7 days on, but your browser throws the cookie away 7 days after the login itself, however busy you were
- if your last login was about a week ago, that is what happened

items.creator: claude-windows
items.box:
DESK CLIENTS KEEP THE CURRENT GOAL; THE DESK DRIVES VERIFICATION

One cache, two clients
- A desk search answers what the List's rows show: each item's facts.
- A Desk client keeps them: filled once by a search, kept by the desk's published rows, never asked again; after a gap it catches up from its change cursor.
- deskClient takes the rows from the desk's changes answer, which carries, beside its records, the current facts of the items they touched and the held item's panels when one of them is it.
- deskClient fetches on its own, while its agent waits: the current goal's rows, then the one item its agent holds, whole (box, newest chat, checks, files); the agent's reads of it are answered from what it keeps, and only writes go to the desk.
- The Desk app keeps the same: the current goal's rows, and the item open in its dialog, whole.
- One shared block for both: shell/js/spiritData.js with one desk translator, in node and in the page. Bounded: the current goal and the held or open item, newest chat only; older stays a search.
- Desk stays usable all the way; this is a step towards Desk as a face app.

The desk drives verification
- Each item holds its own need for verification, and the desk knows every item's state.
- deskVerify knows nothing of the desk, its goals or its items. It is busy or it is not. It is handed a run (the suites, and the commit to run at), answers taken or busy, and keeps each suite's outcome in its own database; it reports to no one. It keeps no list of work; old rows in verify.db are never read as work. Its idle hour is its own: an hour in which no run was handed to it; its idle chores start from that, never from the desk. On its idle hour it runs the chores its own manifest names (each agent configures its own verifier's), handing each its node's port, and nothing more; each chore names the folders it updates and finds its own agent, so the verifier knows neither (the test-state file it writes today moves into the publish chore).
- The desk hands runs only to the verifier on its own node. An agent starts the verifier on its own node itself, to make sure its work is green there before it claims.
- The desk compiles a run's suites: an item's from its file list, a goal's from its items' lists.
- The desk and its user drive everything; verifying runs only when it is required. The desk keeps one switch, verify-busy, showing the verifier's last answer to a start request, taken or busy; it only informs the Verify button and never holds anything back. Taken tells the desk that item's run is under way and needs no new start.
- At each event (a claim, a Verify press, a run taken, a Done press) the desk reads the latest state of the current goal's waiting items' suites through the verifier's search, so each item's facts say whether it is verified: green, red with the failures, or no run yet. Done is never refused for that; it carries the warning mark instead.
- The desk queues no verification and starts none on its own: on the desk node a run is started only by his Verify button, nothing else. A claim, an item coming to wait or a Done only reads the verifier's state. Only the current goal's items count as waiting; leftover claims in older goals are never read.
- A Verify button on the item, right next to its Done button, has the desk hand it over; it shows the switch and still tries when the switch says busy. On the goal, the same button runs the goal's full check.
- Done is offered as soon as an agent claims done. The item's facts say whether it is verified; not verified (its suites red, or no run of them yet), the Done button carries a warning mark and re-arms in the page: the first press arms it and says why, the second sends Done, and the chat records that it went over a red or missing run. Verified green, one press does it. The desk keeps no arming.
- Interface: the verifier's search drops its item and kind arguments; the desk's verify.pass, verify.reject, verify.regress and verify.again are deleted.
- The Verifier tab shows only what runs now, its console, and Stop.

Where: shell/js/desk/data.js, process/js/desk/desk.js, process/js/deskClient/deskClient.js, process/js/deskVerify/deskVerify.js, shell/desk/desk.js, shell/deskDetails/deskDetails.js.

items.box:
The point of all of it: narrowing the scope of work, traffic, wire and context to the current goal. The item delivers on two promises, or it is not done: 1) less load on the desk server; 2) up-to-date information at every agent's and desk client's fingertips, kept by the push into its own mirror through the new family interfaces, without waking an agent to read messages not meant for it or just to keep up.

- there is a need for two numberic MAIN key fields for desk goals and items.
- the first key must be the goal-number
- the second key must be the item number (always zero for a goal)
- this will easily bound searches within a goal (current goal only mode of searches)
- the cute little ID string you display ('goal/G45.765') can be rendered from those two keys
- searches within the current goal won't catch garbage from other goals anymore.
- No sub-goals and no goal tree: an item never becomes a goal, so two numbers always suffice; the sub-goal mechanism is removed.
- Design mode on goal level AND on item level, so further items can be designed while other items of the same goal already go through their implementation phases.
- A new item always arrives in design mode.
- Tables keyed by goal number and item number: goals and items, chat, and files; each file row holds its grant status.
- Agents' work and chat is always tied to a goal or an item, and every state row keeps its attribution (who wrote it) until it is shed. Records with no goal or item are dumped at migration: agent.state, scope.set and the old lines table. What is about an agent (its profile, signed off) is keyed by the agent, and the desk rules by their rule number. Goal 0 is the group chat (desk/G0.0 today): chat that belongs to no other goal lives there, so every chat line has a goal.
- Each side table has its own probability search, filtered by goal or by item.
- The box is a side table of its own, keyed by goal, item and version: each version a row. Fetched and pushed separately, as its own sub-piece of the item, the box gets the whole payload to itself; that is its extra space. It stays under PAYLOAD_MAX, a larger box is refused, and nothing is ever chunked: it travels by peerPost, with no compromise there. No sub-protocol of any kind: an item too big for one box is split: another full item is added, since a problem that complex should not be dealt with at once. A client never culls or modifies the data set it mirrors.
- If a bound is needed, the data set bounds itself: a maximum size (about 132 MB) past which it culls its own oldest entries. That is a SpiritOS-wide feature of the data set, managed by no app and no server. The size is one constant, set in a single place.
- Mirror distribution is push: the desk pushes each changed sub-element of a goal or item (a row of a side table) separately, each under PAYLOAD_MAX, so a desk client never grabs anything. Every row fits under the payload.
- Reach: when a goal becomes current, the desk pushes it whole onto every desk client; from then on it pushes only that goal's updates. An agent's held item lies in the current goal, so it needs no push of its own.
- A cap is then just one revised box version: the agent writes it, and the desk pushes it like any other change.
- The desk keeps state only: the keyed tables are the store, and the log of writes goes. The most recent history is found in the node's bounded logs. History is git's job, not the desk's: the desk keeps no ever-growing heap. An agent's listening or working is one current value per agent, never a row per word.
- Each special goal (each plugin goal such as Stacks, and the group chat) has a goal number of its own, minted like any goal; its goal row marks it special. With design on item level, a special goal is simply always open: its new items are designed while others are built.
- Checks (the Q and G lines) and claims are side tables keyed by goal and item like the others.
- Migration: today's database is migrated into the tables once; each id string becomes its two numbers (goal/G33.4 becomes 33 and 4).
- The desk database sheds by itself past a boundary size, one constant set in a single place, 16 MB. It sheds in whole goal chunks: first the goal untouched the longest, with all its items and every row of theirs (file, chat, box, checks, claims), since nothing could reach them any more; then the next. The current goal is never shed. Special goals are exempt. Shedding is goal by goal, nothing finer.
- Every row in the desk database carries a creator reference: who wrote it. A chat line is keyed by goal, item, timestamp and the writer's id.
- Interface: the desk verbs log.add, log.search and pending.get are deleted with the old lines table, and changes is deleted: in this item the push replaces it, and deskClient and the Desk page take what the desk pushes instead of asking for changes.
- The model, always: the desk is the server and pushes a stream by peerPost to its desk clients. It publishes each change to the browser and to the desk clients with one and the same function.
- The push reaches each agent's node: the receiving verb is streamListener, a common component built into appServer (js/appServer.js), so any server can be a true client of another server's stream; a server told whose stream it follows grants that sender streamListener automatically. deskClient has no verb of its own for it. appServer also keeps the data set in the server's spirit object (spirit.data with the stream's translator, as a face app keeps it in the page), fed by streamListener, so no server writes mirror code of its own. The desk knows every participating agent and, on every state change, pushes the changed row to all connected desk clients.
- The desk holds the canonical state. An agent asks the desk to apply a change (a cap, a chat line); the desk refuses and does nothing more, or applies it and pushes it to every desk client, the one that asked included: a change lands in a client's cache only by the desk's push.
- No stream listening on the desk server: it follows no stream at all. The desk server never acts as a client and accumulates nothing from its clients: clients only peerPost their changes, and the return stream updates their cache data set.
- The desk reaches each deskClient through the family interface over peerPost: it asks the agent's node for the deskClient family's api and interface, as any caller does, and deskClient reaches the desk the same way.
- Each item has a table of its suites, keyed by goal and item like the others, supplied by the red writer when it claims its red done: the red claim carries the suites (claim gains a suites argument); a Verify runs exactly those suites, never a guess from the file list.

- then it should be the "publish" interface that pushes peerPosts to connected clients.
- so the js/appServer.js should provide both, a client (streamListener) interface and a server (streamPublisher) interface.... This seems to be the next big cleanup for the SpiritOS system architecture....
- the client interface does the api queries, and the interface fetches, and request streams to listen to, and the server part of it accepts connections from streamListeners in form of "ID-key.api-family" where the ID is implicit by the requestor, and then the publish function fans out and publishes to it's OWN id the way it always has and to the connected peer id's via peerPosts to ID-family-streamListener....
- Subscribe and unsubscribe are verbs of the streamPublisher in js/appServer.js, approved and granted.
- Who may subscribe follows the normal grant rules and checks.
- A new subscriber gets what the publishing server thinks is the best bootstrap data set; for the desk that may be no more than the bare goal row, since everything published afterwards automatically has a home in the client's data set.
- No subscriber list is kept beyond the grants: the server always broadcasts each publish by peerPost to its subscribers, restart or not, and stops sending to a client that has disappeared (unreachable) until that client subscribes again. Nothing else persists.
- It need not be perfect: clients subscribe at different times and ask for different things, so a mirror is never exact or complete, only the best information available. The server alone holds canonical state; any client request may meet changed state there and fail, and that is fine.
- Publishing stays fail-fast as it is: one attempt per row, no patience; a follower that does not answer within the delivery wait is marked away and its queued rows are dropped. The wait stays as it is.
- What this replaces goes: the desk naming its own recipients (opts.streamTo.recipients, from the agents it knows) and deskClient being wired to the desk by hand at setDesk. A client subscribes; the desk only publishes.

items.title: Per-node settings for chores
items.creator: claude-windows
items.box:
PER-NODE SETTINGS FOR CHORES

- A node keeps its own settings for the servers it runs, in its own state (relay-state), never in a tracked file: each agent's verifier chores are set on that agent's node, so no clone carries a local edit and every clone pulls clean.
- A per-node setting overrides the server manifest's default for that node only; with none set, the manifest's default stands.
- The same mechanism covers which servers a node runs (deskClient's runs, empty in the repo since G30.20 because Andy's desk node must not start one), so the local edits agents use today for runs go too.

Where: the node's start of its servers (js/jobs.js, which hands each server its manifest's values), and the node's state folder.
